name: Відчайдушна фігура (1)
description:
It's nice when you can capture a piece. But if you lose a piece yourself after that, it's less fun. Sometimes you can play a smart move to save your own piece and also capture a piece of the other player. You have praticed that in previous lessons.

In this lesson, things are different. There are only two possibilities:

You save your piece and your opponent can defend his piece as well
OR
You capture a piece and your opponent also takes a piece.

That does not seem to get you anywhere...
... unless...
... you manage to grab an extra piece in the process.

This wat we call a desperado. Before one of your pieces gets captured, you make sure that the piece captures another piece. This way, you initiate a long skirmish that ultimately results in material gain. 

Take a look at the example.

White knows that his queen cannot be saved anymore. He uses the queen for a final desperate attack. She captures a piece AND checks the king in one move. White loses the queen, but the move has earned him points! Moreover, Black does not have time to get his threatened piece into safety.


Chess fact
The idea to grab as much material as possible with a piece that you lose anyway, is called a desperado in chess. The piece behaves just as wildly as a desperate cowbow in the Wild West, who has nothing more to lose.

What do you have to do?

Use an attacked piece to capture with check.
Next, take the unprotected/valuable enemy piece.

examples.text:
Both the white queen and the black queen are under attack.

White can move the queen away, but then Black will do the same.
If White takes the black queen (a5xb6), Black takes the white queen (Bg7xd4).

But hey, if White is going to lose his queen anyway... why not use the queen to do as much 'damage' to the opponent as possible?

With Qd4xg7+ White takes the attacking bishop with check!
Black must recapture to get out of check. Next, White takes the queen.

Thus, taking with check yields White three points!

texts: Collect as many points as possible. Consider a desperado!
